subject: mathematics
question_text: In a △ABC, if 1/(a+c) + 1/(b+c) = 3/(a+b+c), then show that C = 60°.

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.77 — SAQ chapter 13 Properties of Triangles, answer 86. Printed appearances: TS 17,19. The only question in the chapter that FINDS an angle rather than proving an identity. Everything is algebra until the very last line, where the cosine rule turns a side relation into an angle. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed against this answer. It is not a bare guess: the same book prints 1+1+1+1 for the 4-mark answers 58 and 59 on book p.63 and 1+2+1 for answer 61 on p.64, so both shapes used in this unit are the book's own. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B runs Q11-Q17 at 4 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q17 is the Properties of Triangles slot. Together with Q24 (LAQ) this unit holds TWO slots — one of only two units to do so, Matrices being the other.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — name each standard result you use and the order you use them in.

steps.label: Clear the fractions
steps.margin_note: Half the marks. Combine the left side over one denominator, then cross-multiply. Nothing trigonometric happens yet — this is ordinary algebra.

recall.must_convey: That the left side is combined over one denominator, the numerator written as (a+b+c) + c, and the equation cross-multiplied.
accept: combine the fractions and notice the numerator is a plus b plus c plus another c then cross multiply
put over a common denominator and cross multiply
the numerator becomes the perimeter plus c
common denominator teeskoni cross multiply cheyyali

steps.why: Writing b + c + a + c as (a+b+c) + c is the move that makes the cross-multiplication land on a recognisable expansion rather than a mess.
common_mistakes: Adding the fractions by adding numerators and denominators.

steps.label: Expand and simplify
steps.margin_note: Third mark. Expand both sides fully. Everything cancels except a² + b² − c² = ab — a pure side relation with no fractions left.

recall.must_convey: That both sides expand and cancel down to a² + b² − c² = ab.
accept: expand both sides and everything cancels leaving a squared plus b squared minus c squared equals a b
the algebra reduces to a side relation
it simplifies to a squared plus b squared minus c squared equals ab
expand cheste a square plus b square minus c square equals ab vasthundi
heard_as: a squared plus b squared minus c squared

steps.why: a² + b² − c² is exactly the numerator of the cosine rule for C. Reaching that expression is the signal that the angle is one step away.

steps.label: Apply the cosine rule
steps.margin_note: Last mark. Divide both sides by 2ab: the left becomes cos C exactly, and the right becomes 1/2.

recall.must_convey: That dividing by 2ab gives cos C = 1/2, so C = 60°.
accept: divide by two a b so the left is cos C and the right is a half giving C equals sixty degrees
the cosine rule turns it into cos C equals a half
two ab tho divide cheste cos C half, C sixty degrees

steps.why: Dividing by 2ab is chosen precisely because it makes the left side the cosine rule. Any other division would leave something unrecognisable.
common_mistakes: Stopping at a² + b² − c² = ab.
Writing cos C = 1/2 and giving C = 30°.
